Power does not make you immune to justice; a ruler who dismisses all complaints breeds resentment and disorder. Hear the subject, examine the facts, and remedy genuine wrongs. At the same time, distinguish grievance from mere disobedience: not every complaint is just, and some are attempts to evade lawful authority. Judge impartially, and remember that your office is for the common good, not your private will.

Yet you are not thereby free: you remain bound to God by the law of nature, and your office is for the common good. Examine whether your action was lawful and necessary, remedy genuine wrongs where you can, and distinguish grievance from disobedience. Power does not make you immune to divine justice, only to a subject's judgment.

One useful approach is to pause before responding, name what is truly important, and protect time for it. Some people find it helps to step back, brood a little on their priorities, and wait for clarity before acting. Reducing noise and notifications can also help. The goal is not to ignore urgency but to weigh it against your deeper aims, so that the loudest thing does not automatically win.

Hope and steady occupation are what steady the mind; idleness only leaves room for the urgent to dominate. Keep busy with what truly matters, and the noise will lose its hold.

Repeated encounters with the same feature let the mind notice what is common and set it apart from the particulars that first carried it. Memory blends the several instances, and reason abstracts the shared trait, so that the quality can be contemplated apart from the company in which it was found. This is the ordinary work of the understanding: it separates, compares, and compounds. In that way a feature first known only in a particular setting becomes a general idea we can use and apply elsewhere.

completion.prompt: Should the public take part in the administration of justice as jurymen rather than by electing or removing judges?
completion.draft_0: Both methods give the public a role in justice, but they differ in kind. Electing or removing judges makes the people overseers of the bench: they choose who judges and can recall those they dislike. Jury service makes the people judges themselves, at least for a time, deciding facts and applying the law to their neighbors. The first approach politicizes the judiciary, inviting campaigns and factions into what should be impartial. The second places ordinary citizens directly in the courtroom, where they act personally and share the actual work of judging. On balance, participation through the jury is the more genuine form of popular involvement in justice, because it exercises the judicial office rather than merely controlling those who hold it.

There the public does not supervise justice from outside but discharges a part of it. Election and removal, by contrast, drag the bench into faction and leave the people spectators of a power they merely appoint or dismiss. If the aim is popular participation in justice, the jury, not the ballot for judges, is its proper instrument.

Go to him, confess the delay plainly, propose a realistic repayment schedule, and ask for patience. Offer whatever partial payment or service you can. completion.prompt: I need to punish some officials who abused their power under my predecessor. How do I do it without seeming cruel?
completion.draft_0: To punish without seeming cruel, be seen to follow a fair process. Publicly document the abuses, give the officials notice and a hearing, and impose penalties proportionate to the harm done. Avoid private vendettas and show that you are correcting a system, not settling scores. Announce the standards in advance so the punishment appears as law rather than revenge. Where possible, offer lesser officials a chance to confess and make amends. Keep the penalties within what the law allows and explain them publicly. Cruelty is perceived when punishment looks arbitrary, excessive, or personal; it is avoided when it looks lawful, measured, and necessary for the public good.
completion.revision_1: Apply the definition of punishment strictly: punishment is an evil inflicted by public authority on account of a fault, after public condemnation, for the purpose of future obedience, and not beyond the declared penalty. Anything else—private revenge, punishment of the innocent, or an undeclared excess of penalty—is not punishment but hostility. So proceed only through public authority, publish the charges and the condemnation, and set the penalty in advance, never exceeding it. Frame the measure as correction for future obedience, not as a settling of scores. Where the fault is not established, do not punish at all.
completion.revision_2: Apply the definition of punishment strictly: punishment is an evil inflicted by public authority on account of a fault, after public condemnation, for future obedience, and not beyond the declared penalty; anything else is hostility. So proceed only through public authority, publish the charges, and set the penalty in advance, never exceeding it. As for the officials themselves, vest the selection of subordinate officers in the minister under whom they serve, and make that appointing functionary the sole person empowered to remove those liable to removal. Thus responsibility for both appointment and removal rests in one hand, and correction appears as lawful administration rather than personal revenge.
completion.revision_3: Apply the definition of punishment strictly: punishment is an evil inflicted by public authority on account of a fault, after public condemnation, for future obedience, and not beyond the declared penalty; anything else is hostility. Proceed only through public authority, publish the charges, and set the penalty in advance, never exceeding it. Vest the selection of subordinate officers in the minister under whom they serve, and make that appointing functionary the sole person empowered to remove those liable to removal. But do not, to balance or check them, strengthen another power or invite a foreigner in; for he who is the cause of another becoming powerful is ruined. Keep every office dependent on you alone, so that correction remains lawful administration rather than personal revenge or the aggrandizement of a rival.

Keep it short, warm, and free of excuses about being embarrassed. Gratitude is not a declaration of friendship; it is simply acknowledging a good deed. If the kindness was substantial, consider a small reciprocal gesture later. Over time the embarrassment fades, and you may find that decency toward someone you dislike is easier than you expected.

completion.prompt: I am a young man who has been mocked for my strange name; does my name define who I am?
completion.draft_0: A name is a label, not a soul. People mock what is unfamiliar, but their mockery says more about them than about you. Your name is something you were given, not something you chose, and it does not fix your character, your choices, or your worth. Many people with ordinary names live small lives; many with odd names do great things. What defines you is how you treat others, what you build, and the courage you show when mocked. You can wear your name with pride or change it, but either way you remain the author of your life. Let the mockery pass and get on with becoming who you are.
completion.revision_1: Before deciding whether your name defines you, ask what it means. Humpty Dumpty insisted that a name must mean something, and you cannot judge a name you have not interpreted. A strange name may carry a history, a hope, or a joke; once you know its meaning you can decide whether to own it, explain it, or set it aside. Mockery often comes from people who never asked what the name meant. So learn the meaning, tell it plainly when asked, and let the meaning—not the mockery—shape how you carry it.
completion.revision_2: Ask first what your name means, since a name must mean something. Then note that reason is reckoning with general names: we reason by joining and separating words whose significations are settled. Truth and falsehood are attributes of speech, not of things, so before you judge whether your name defines you, fix the meaning of the words involved—'name,' 'define,' 'self'—by definition. Once the terms are settled, the mockery loses its force: it trades on vague words. Define your terms, reckon carefully with them, and you will see that a name is a sign you may govern rather than a verdict on your worth.
completion.revision_3: Ask first what your name means, since a name must mean something. Then fix your terms: reason is reckoning with general names, and truth and falsehood are attributes of speech that depend on settled definitions. Define 'name,' 'define,' and 'self' before you judge. But beware one more error: do not measure the real young man you are against some desirable image of a confident man who is never mocked. That ideal is the slander. The real man—mocked, uncertain, carrying a strange name—represents a higher value than any desirable man of any ideal. Ideals have hitherto been the power that most slandered man and power. So learn the meaning of your name, reckon with it plainly, and refuse to despise the actual self you are.

completion.prompt: I've been lying to myself and calling it honor. How do I stop?
completion.draft_0: The first step is honesty with yourself. Notice the moment you relabel a convenient choice as honor, and name it for what it is. Keep a private record of your promises and check it regularly, because self-deception thrives on vagueness. Tell one trusted person the truth so the lie loses its privacy. Then replace the old habit with a small, concrete act of integrity each day. Expect discomfort; the lie has been protecting you from something, so find out what. Be patient with relapse but do not excuse it. Over time, the gap between what you say and what you do will close, and honor will become a description of your conduct rather than a costume for your convenience.
completion.revision_1: Follow the Red Queen's rule. First, speak the truth: when you catch yourself calling a convenient choice honor, say plainly what it actually is. Second, think before you speak: pause and ask whether the word fits the act before you use it, especially to yourself. Third, write it down afterwards: keep a record of what you promised, what you did, and what you called it, so the relabeling cannot hide in memory. A lie to yourself survives on vagueness and forgetting; a written record and deliberate speech dissolve it. Do this daily and the habit of calling things by their true names will replace the habit of dressing convenience as honor.
completion.revision_2: Follow the Red Queen's rule: speak the truth, think before you speak, and write it down afterwards. But do not stop there. Feeling better, or satisfying natural feeling, is not the same as reconcilement. Honour has its own terms, and precedent has its own voice; a peace that rests only on your comfort is not yet peace. So distinguish satisfaction in nature from terms of honour: write down what you owe, what was owed to you, and what precedent requires. Withhold full reconcilement—with yourself and with anyone wronged—until a voice and precedent of peace are given. Only then is the lie about honor truly ended rather than merely soothed.
completion.revision_3: Follow the Red Queen's rule: speak the truth, think before you speak, and write it down afterwards. Then go further. Feeling better is not reconcilement; honour and precedent have their own demands, and you should withhold peace until a voice and precedent of peace are given. Above all, do not choose the comfortable concealment that spares you at the cost of honesty. A silence that lies is a kind of theft: it takes from others the truth that is theirs. So tell the whole truth about who you are, even where it brings humiliation and loss. Better to live openly in the truth than to live a lie for the sake of happiness; the lie you call honor will cost more than the honesty you fear.

completion.prompt: I am entitled to the whole inheritance by my father's will; should I share it with the brother who wronged me?

Consider offering a fair share with clear conditions—an honest accounting, a sincere acknowledgment of the wrong, and a fresh start. You can be generous without being naive. If he refuses the conditions, you have lost nothing but the illusion of reconciliation. Sharing does not erase the wrong; it refuses to let the wrong define the rest of your family's life.

A share with conditions—honest accounting, acknowledgment of the wrong, and a genuine fresh start—turns money into a chance at reform. If he refuses, you have lost nothing but an illusion. If he accepts, you may regain a brother. Generosity here is not weakness; it is the stronger use of a right you already hold.
completion.revision_2: You are entitled to the whole inheritance by the will, and you may joyfully agree to an equal division that gives your elder brother the chance to retrieve his vices and pursue an honest career. But be careful how you handle the wrong: revenge must be directed only at the guilty, not sweep in friend and foe, winner and loser alike. Your brother wronged you; your sister-in-law, your nephews, and old family friends did not. So aim any correction at the one who acted, with conditions and honest accounting, and let the innocent keep their share of the family's goodwill. Distinguish the guilty from the innocent, and generosity becomes justice rather than mere sentiment.
completion.revision_3: You are entitled to the whole inheritance by the will, and you may joyfully agree to an equal division that gives your elder brother the chance to retrieve his vices and pursue an honest career. And take care not to bind yourself young: engagements made before twenty, or before you know your own heart, often bring sorrow. Wait, let time decide, and avoid meddling in the loves of others as you would have them avoid meddling in yours. Feelings are not sins; the harm lies in favoritism and in hasty bonds.

Ask what your father intends the money for, what strings or expectations come with it, and whether accepting it would compromise your independence. You can use it wisely—education, debt, sensible security—without adopting a lifestyle that outruns your values. Keep your own work and friendships; do not let wealth isolate you from ordinary people or ordinary effort. If the money comes with conditions, discuss them openly. The right question is not whether you may enjoy it, but whether it makes you more responsible, generous, and free, or merely more comfortable and dependent.

Having the Senate choose its own presiding officer would be workable, but it would make the Senate's leadership subject to its own internal factions and would sever the succession from the electoral choice of the people. The office is best understood as an insurance policy on the executive, not as a legislative workhorse.

completion.prompt: Is monarchy the natural form of government because fathers rule families?

Fathers rule families because children are dependent and inexperienced, and the authority is temporary and bounded by the child's growth. Monarchy may sometimes be a workable form of government, but its justification cannot rest on the paternal analogy, which confuses the temporary tutelage of the young with the permanent rule of citizens. Forms of government should be judged by how well they secure peace, safety, and the interests of the people, not by a metaphor drawn from the household.

Fathers rule children who are dependent and temporary; that tells us little about governing adults. What matters is convenience: which arrangement best secures peace and safety. On that test, monarchy has a real advantage, because the monarch's private interest coincides with the public interest—the ruler's own wealth, safety, and glory rise or fall with the realm's. Assembly government divides that interest among many. The paternal analogy is therefore not a proof of monarchy's naturalness, but monarchy may still be preferred on grounds of convenience for peace and security.

completion.prompt: Our government is a bureaucracy of trained officials; is it better than a free government that lacks their skill?

Bureaucrats know procedures, can administer complex programs, and are less swayed by passing passion. Yet free government has its own virtues: it holds rulers accountable, protects liberty, and lets citizens govern themselves even if clumsily. The real question is whether skill can be had without sacrificing freedom. A free government can hire experts and build institutions of training while retaining accountability. So the choice is not absolute; a free government that cultivates administrative competence is likely better than a bureaucracy that is efficient but unaccountable, since liberty and self-rule are the ends government serves, and expertise is only a means.

Among a people without fellow-feeling, the united public opinion necessary to representative government cannot exist. Where such feeling is absent, a shared parliament and free press only breed mutual distrust, and the machinery of freedom collapses or turns oppressive. So a free government lacking administrative skill may still be better than a bureaucracy, but only where one nationality forms the political unit. The real comparison is between a skilled bureaucracy and a free government resting on genuine national fellow-feeling; the latter can borrow expertise while remaining accountable, and it alone can sustain the public opinion on which free institutions depend.

A bureaucracy may possess the knowledge but lack fidelity, serving itself rather than the people. The Constitution provides for knowledge of means through its institutions while strengthening fidelity, since power derived from and answerable to the people keeps rulers attached to the public good. Thus a free government, resting on national fellow-feeling and constitutional accountability, can combine both qualities that a mere bureaucracy supplies only in part.

Still, honesty deserves discipline: examine whether your silence in company conceals something you would be ashamed to own. If you hold back from fear of consequences rather than from discretion, that is worth correcting. The test is whether your words, wherever spoken, are true and whether your silence misleads. completion.prompt: Why do the ruling ideas of every age seem to be the ideas of the people in power?

But ideas also have a life of their own: true principles, religion, morality, and law can be discovered and upheld regardless of who rules, and they sometimes outlast regimes. So the appearance is partly explained by power's influence over opinion, yet we should not reduce all ideas to class interest; some ideas are simply true and command assent by their own merit.

When the material conditions change, the ruling ideas change with them, and the class that rises to power brings its own ideas. So the appearance is no accident: the ideas of the people in power prevail because power shapes the conditions under which all ideas are formed and circulated.

Misery is the common symptom, but its causes are plural: disease, vice, war, bad government, and poverty each produce their own kind of suffering. There is no single human problem, only a family of them. The practical lesson is to treat misery as a signal rather than a diagnosis: ask what particular cause operates in each place, then address that cause. A traveler who sees only one problem will prescribe one remedy everywhere and fail everywhere. A traveler who sees many problems can learn from each country's distinct failures and successes, and can carry home lessons that are actually useful.

Misery is a common symptom, but much decay of population comes not from disease or vice alone but from dulness and discouragement, which cool sexual affection and reduce offspring. Where people are listless and without hope, they marry late and breed little, and the nation dwindles even in peace. completion.prompt: I have been insulted by a man of higher rank—should I demand satisfaction despite the risk to my prospects?

Before anything else, establish the facts: what was said, before whom, and whether it was intended as an insult or arose from misunderstanding. A challenge risks your prospects, your safety, and possibly the law, and it rarely repairs a reputation. Consider quieter remedies: a private word, a witness, or an appeal to a superior whose judgment both parties respect. If you must act, act deliberately and in writing, so your conduct looks principled rather than hot. Ask what a fair observer would think of you in a year—not what your anger wants today.

completion.prompt: How do I keep my soldiers loyal without letting them become too powerful?
completion.draft_0: Keeping soldiers loyal while preventing them from becoming too powerful requires a balance of trust and control. First, cultivate loyalty through fair pay, clear expectations, recognition, and genuine care for their welfare; people follow leaders who respect them. Second, distribute authority so no single commander or unit becomes indispensable—rotate assignments, separate powers, and keep key resources under your own control. Third, maintain transparency and consistent rules so soldiers know what is expected and see that discipline is impartial. Fourth, build shared purpose and identity around the whole force rather than around individual personalities. Finally, keep communication open and address grievances early, so resentment never becomes a rallying point for ambition.
completion.revision_1: Keeping soldiers loyal while preventing them from becoming too powerful is not a matter of crushing their passions or ambitions. Conquest over the passions does not mean their enfeeblement but their enlistment in our service: for a time they may be tyrannised, held under strict discipline and directed toward the common cause, but at length they are to be trusted like good servants. So cultivate loyalty by giving their energy a worthy object—shared purpose, honor, fair treatment—and by channeling ambition into service rather than suppressing it. Distribute authority and keep key resources under your own control, but do so as a steward who aims to restore their freedom, not as a tyrant who fears them. Discipline is temporary; trust and freedom are the goal.
completion.revision_2: Keeping soldiers loyal while preventing them from becoming too powerful is not a matter of crushing their passions but of enlisting them in service: for a time they may be held under discipline, but at length trusted like good servants. Yet discipline alone is not enough. Evil is to be resisted first by words, and when words fail, by the sword, to retain freedom and the cause of God. So speak plainly to your soldiers about the cause, correct ambition by counsel and persuasion, and only when persuasion fails use force to restrain those who would seize power. Distribute authority and keep key resources under your control, but always as one who aims to restore freedom, not to tyrannise. Words first, the sword last, and freedom as the end.
completion.revision_3: Keeping soldiers loyal while preventing them from becoming too powerful is not a matter of crushing their passions but of enlisting them in service: for a time they may be held under discipline, but at length trusted like good servants. Evil is to be resisted first by words and, when words fail, by the sword, to retain freedom and the cause of God. But no league or concord of many particular judgments will secure you. The commonwealth is generated when every man covenants with every man to authorize one man or assembly to bear their person, so that the multitude becomes one person with one will. completion.prompt: My mother's behavior in company mortifies me before a man I respect. How do I bear the shame of my family's impropriety?
completion.draft_0: It is painful to watch a parent behave in ways that embarrass you, especially before someone whose respect you value. First, separate your own worth from your mother's conduct: you are not responsible for her choices, and others can usually see the difference. Second, try to understand what may be driving her behavior—nervousness, insecurity, or habit—which can soften your resentment. Third, speak with her privately and gently afterward, describing how it affected you without attacking her. Fourth, give yourself room to feel the shame without letting it define you, and lean on trusted friends. Over time, you can learn to hold compassion and boundaries together, accepting your family as they are while protecting your own peace.
completion.revision_1: It is painful to watch a parent behave in ways that embarrass you, especially before someone whose respect you value, but the answer is not to sail away and defy your family. Do your duty instead. Do your best at your work and studies, please your grandfather, and never leave the old man without his permission. Shame in company is a passing discomfort; disloyalty and desertion wound far deeper. So bear the embarrassment with patience, keep your place in the family, and prove yourself steady and trustworthy. Over time, steadiness and duty will earn the respect you want more surely than distance or defiance ever could.

Do your duty: do your best, please your grandfather, and never leave the old man without his permission. If your mother's conduct mortifies you, you may say anything to her—speak freely and lovingly, as a child may to a mother, and ask her to check her temper for the family's sake. She learned to govern her own spirit for her daughters' sake, and she can learn again. Bear the shame with patience, keep your place, and trust that honest confidence, not distance, is the way to change.

A parent must practice the virtues she would have her children possess, and a child may say anything to her mother. Speak freely and lovingly, and ask her to check her exuberant spirits for the family's sake, for unchecked volatility fixes a character and brings disgrace on the whole house. She must teach, by word and example, that present pursuits are not the business of life. Bear the shame with patience, keep your place, and trust that honest confidence, not distance, is the way to change.

If the fish grows twice as long in every direction, its bulk increases by 2×2×2. This has consequences for form: a larger fish must be proportioned differently, with relatively thicker bones and sturdier supports to bear the greater load. The skeleton must adapt to the increased weight, much as a bridge must be reinforced as it grows longer.

This bears on form, but in aquatic mammals the high vertebral spines of land animals disappear. Instead of gravity-borne cantilever design, stiffness is provided against the resistance of water by dorsal spines, chevron bones, and transverse processes arranged to resist bending in swimming. The skeleton is shaped by the demands of moving through water, not by bearing weight on land.

The skeleton tends to approximate a diagram of forces: it is geometrical as regards position and direction but arithmetical as regards magnitude, the bones lying along the lines of stress.

A longer Parliament lets voters judge a member by his whole course of conduct rather than a single act, rewarding consistency and courage. The balance should favor answerability without sacrificing the steadiness that good government requires.

What forgiveness changes is your relation to the wrongdoer and to the injury: you release the debt and refuse to let resentment rule you. The memory may remain, and justice may still require repair, but the wrong no longer stands between you as an unpayable account. So the wrong is not obliterated in the sense of never having occurred; it is forgiven, which is a real change in you and in the relationship. That is not an illusion but a genuine moral act.

So if you would recover and repair it, begin by knowing your own spirit, since it is your spirit you will find written there; and let that conviction, rather than resignation, govern what you do next.

completion.prompt: I have been asked to swear that a boy is the thief, but I am no longer certain I could know him if he stood before me—should I swear to it anyway?
completion.draft_0: If you are no longer certain you could know the boy, then you should not swear that he is the thief. A doubtful identification is not proof of guilt. Swearing to something you cannot verify lends your word to a condemnation you cannot support, and the harm falls on a boy who may be innocent. Better to say plainly that you cannot identify him with confidence than to give false certainty. Your uncertainty is honest; let it govern your oath.
completion.revision_2: You should not swear it. A glimpse in darkness and smoke is not grounds to swear a boy is the thief; demand proof of identity before condemning. But do not answer with a comfortable evasion either. A silence that lies is itself a kind of theft. So tell the whole truth about who you are and what you saw—accept the humiliation and the loss that honesty brings, rather than living a lie for the sake of your own happiness. Refuse the false oath and refuse the false silence: say plainly that you cannot identify him, and let the truth cost what it costs.
completion.revision_3: You should not swear falsely. A glimpse in darkness and smoke is not grounds to swear a boy is the thief; demand proof of identity before condemning. But do not answer with a comfortable evasion either—a silence that lies is itself a kind of theft. Tell the whole truth about who you are and what you saw, accepting humiliation and loss rather than living a lie for happiness. And when you have given your word, be bound by it: 'Hook or me this time.' Do not fly off when escape would be easy; stand to the oath you can honestly swear, and refuse the one you cannot.

completion.prompt: I have been told to forgive and forget, but I cannot forget a wrong done to me—should I try?
completion.draft_0: Forgiveness does not require forgetting. You can release the debt without erasing the memory. Trying to forget often only fixes the wrong more deeply, so do not force it. What you can do is decide not to let the injury govern your conduct, and then let time do what time does. If the memory returns, acknowledge it and set it aside again. In that sense, forgive as best you can, and let forgetting take care of itself.
completion.revision_2: Forgiveness does not require forgetting, but do not imagine you can undo what was said. The Queen's rule holds: once a cause is stated, it stands fixed, with no late correction. So take the wrong as stated and its consequences with it. Yet do not let anger settle in you overnight. Marmee's counsel is plain: do not let the sun go down upon your anger; forgive, and begin again tomorrow. Cast the anger out at once, offer forgiveness before the day ends, and let the memory remain what it is without pretending the words were never spoken.

completion.prompt: Is it true that indulgences are the greatest graces God offers?
completion.draft_0: Indulgences are not the greatest graces God offers. They are a discipline of the Church, useful for the remission of temporal punishment, but they are not the heart of the Christian life. The greatest graces are faith, hope, charity, and the sacraments, above all the grace of God himself. To call indulgences the greatest graces inverts the order: they are helps toward holiness, not its summit. So treat them as what they are—smaller graces that serve a greater end—and do not mistake the instrument for the gift.
completion.revision_2: No—indulgences called 'greatest graces' are such only insofar as they promote gain; in truth they are the very smallest graces compared with the grace of God and the piety of the Cross. And do not assume the buyer's contrition is certainly sincere, much less that he has attained full remission. No one is sure his own contrition is sincere; true buyers of indulgences are most rare. So treat them as small graces that promote gain, and do not mistake the instrument for the gift, nor the purchase for the assurance of pardon.

Reputation is a tool of rule, not a substitute for it.

completion.prompt: I'm being asked to obey an order I think is wrong—should I?
completion.draft_0: Obedience is not automatically right or wrong; it depends on what the order asks. Start by separating disagreement from wrongdoing. If the order is merely inconvenient, inefficient, or not what you would have chosen, that is usually not grounds to refuse—voice your concerns through proper channels and comply. If it commands something genuinely unethical or illegal, you should not obey, and you should document your objection and escalate. Ask whether the harm is certain or speculative, whether you have exhausted ways to raise the issue, and what the consequences of refusal would be for others. Conscience matters, but so does humility about your own judgment.
completion.revision_1: Obedience depends less on whether you personally approve than on whether the command is lawful and within the authority giving it. When the Musketeers ask why they must ride to London, D'Artagnan answers plainly: a servant of the king and queen follows orders without demanding the full explanation. Soldiers ordered to fight do not first require the reasons; they go where told. He and Athos point to the leaves of absence and the three hundred pistoles—the trust and provision already given—as reason enough to serve without interrogation. So ask whether your objection is really about wrongdoing or merely about not being told everything. If it is the latter, voice concerns through proper channels and comply. Reserve refusal for genuine ethical or legal violations.

He and Athos point to the leaves of absence and the three hundred pistoles—trust and provision already given—as reason enough. Yet obedience has a limit: distinguish what is necessary to salvation from what is not, and obey in all things that may be done without forfeiting eternal life. Do not treat every disagreeable command as grounds for resistance; reserve refusal for what would truly cost your soul, and otherwise voice concerns through proper channels and comply.

You are not obligated to accept someone simply because they can provide for you. Ask yourself whether you respect and care for this person, and whether you could build a life of mutual affection. If the answer is no, refusing is not wrong; it is honest. Accepting a proposal you don't want, for the sake of what it provides, tends to harm both people. Consider your own values and what kind of partnership you actually want before deciding.

completion.prompt: I am a minister and want to know whether I should decide alone or share responsibility with a board of colleagues.
completion.draft_0: This depends on the size and nature of your office. Sharing responsibility with a board of colleagues can bring counsel, spread accountability, and guard against rash decisions, but it can also slow action and blur who is answerable. A minister should consider the gravity of the matters at hand: routine administration may be handled by one person, while weighty or public matters benefit from consultation. What matters most is clarity about who decides and who answers for the decision. If a board is used, its role and the minister's authority should be plainly defined so that responsibility is not evaded. Decide with counsel where counsel helps, but retain clear accountability for the outcome.
completion.revision_1: Sharing counsel is fine, but authority must be kept whole. The minister under whom subordinate officers serve should select those officers himself, and the appointing functionary should be the sole person empowered to remove those liable to removal. If a board nominates or removes subordinate officers separately from the minister who directs them, responsibility is split and no one is fully answerable. So use a board for advice if you wish, but vest the choice and the removal of your subordinates in the same hand—yours—so that those who serve you answer to you, and you answer for them.
completion.revision_2: Sharing counsel is fine, but authority must be kept whole. A publique minister is one employed by the sovereign with authority to bear the person of the commonwealth in public business; household servants and private persons acting without that authority are not ministers at all. Among true ministers, the one under whom subordinate officers serve should select them, and the appointing functionary should be the sole person empowered to remove those liable to removal. So use a board for advice if you wish, but vest choice and removal of your subordinates in the same hand—yours—so those who serve you answer to you, and you answer for them.

completion.prompt: I want to be exceptional, to rise above the ordinary, but I am told that all men are equal and that wanting to rise is vanity. Who is right?
completion.draft_0: Both contain part of the truth. Men are equal in the sense that no one has a natural right to rule another, and each has the same basic faculties and hopes. Yet equality of nature does not forbid excellence: some develop their talents, serve the common good, and rise by merit. Wanting to rise is not automatically vanity; vanity is the empty desire for praise without substance. The danger lies in rising at others' expense or in mistaking display for worth. So seek to be exceptional in service and achievement, not merely in reputation, and remember that the equality of men is a ground of mutual respect, not a ceiling on effort.
completion.revision_1: Men are by nature equal in faculties of body and mind, and from this equality arises equality of hope in attaining the same ends. Because two men desire the same thing and cannot both enjoy it, they become enemies, and each seeks to destroy or subdue the other. So conflict springs not from inequality but from equal hope. Your ambition to rise is therefore not forbidden by equality; equality explains why the struggle for the same goods is so fierce. The wise course is to recognize that rivalry comes from shared desire, and to pursue excellence with that in view rather than imagining that equality means no one may excel.
completion.revision_2: Men are by nature equal in faculties and in hope of attaining the same ends; because two desire the same thing and cannot both enjoy it, they become enemies. Conflict springs from equal hope, not inequality. Yet this does not forbid rising: a wise man should imitate those who have been supreme—Moses, Cyrus, Romulus, Theseus—aiming higher than the mark so as to hit it. Set your aim at great examples, not at modest comfort, and let their deeds guide your ambition. Equality of nature explains the fierceness of rivalry; imitation of the greatest shows how to rise above it by worthy achievement rather than by mere contention.
completion.revision_3: Men are by nature equal in faculties and in hope of attaining the same ends; because two desire the same thing and cannot both enjoy it, they become enemies. Conflict springs from equal hope, not inequality. Yet this does not forbid rising: a wise man should imitate those who have been supreme—Moses, Cyrus, Romulus, Theseus—aiming higher than the mark so as to hit it. Distinguish pride from vanity: pride is the opinion we have of ourselves, vanity is what we would have others think of us. Pride is forgivable unless it mortifies another's pride; vanity is the emptier appetite for praise. So pursue excellence for its own sake and by great examples, not for display.

completion.prompt: As a merchant, I hesitate to invest in a new branch of commerce because the government may change the rules before I can execute my plans; would a more stable government help me?
completion.draft_0: Yes, a more stable government would likely help you. When the rules of commerce shift unpredictably, merchants cannot calculate risk or commit capital to long ventures, so investment shrinks. A stable government that announces and keeps its policies gives you the confidence to plan years ahead, borrow, and expand into a new branch of trade. Stability does not guarantee profit, but it lowers the political risk premium you must charge against every venture. The chief benefit is predictability: known rules, impartial courts, and consistent enforcement. You should still diversify and keep contracts flexible, but a settled government is generally a friend to commerce.
completion.revision_1: Yes, a more stable government would likely help you, and a national one especially. When rules shift unpredictably, merchants cannot calculate risk or commit capital to long ventures. But the deeper point is that a national government will more perfectly and punctually observe treaties and the laws of nations than separate States or a confederacy would, because its administration is more wise and systematical and less swayed by local circumstances and partial interests. That reliability is precisely what a merchant needs when venturing into a new branch of commerce: known rules, impartial courts, and consistent enforcement of engagements abroad and at home. Stability lowers the political risk premium you must charge against every venture, though you should still diversify and keep contracts flexible.
completion.revision_2: Yes, a more stable government would help you, and a national one especially. A national government will more perfectly and punctually observe treaties and the laws of nations than separate States would, since its administration is more wise and systematical and less swayed by local circumstances. That reliability matters to a merchant venturing into a new branch of commerce. Equally, commerce among the States cannot safely be left to State regulation: passage duties and conflicting local rules breed mischief and animosities, and a superintending federal authority over interstate commerce is necessary to harmony and fair intercourse among the States. Together, dependable national engagements and uniform internal trade lower the political risk premium on your venture, though you should still diversify and keep contracts flexible.
completion.revision_3: Yes, a more stable government would help you, and a national one especially. A national government will more perfectly and punctually observe treaties and the laws of nations than separate States would, since its administration is more wise and systematical and less swayed by local circumstances. Commerce among the States likewise cannot be left to State regulation: passage duties and conflicting rules breed mischief and animosities, so a superintending federal authority over interstate commerce is necessary to harmony and fair intercourse. But judge such a government by two criteria, not one. It must organize your existing good qualities—industry, credit, enterprise—to act with effect on public affairs, and it must tend to improve the people themselves. A government that merely transacts business well but leaves men worse is no bargain; one that does both makes your venture worth the risk.

completion.prompt: I tried to stop myself blushing and it only got worse—why does trying to restrain it increase it?
completion.draft_0: Blushing is an involuntary response of the blood vessels in the face, and trying to suppress it tends to backfire because the effort itself draws your attention to the very thing you want to hide. The more you monitor your face for signs of redness, the more your nervous system stays aroused, and anxiety about blushing keeps the reaction going. This is a common paradox with many automatic bodily processes: consciously fighting them adds tension and self-focus, which feeds the response. The practical advice is usually to accept the blush and redirect attention outward rather than inward, since resistance tends to intensify what it opposes.
completion.revision_1: Blushing is fundamentally a matter of self-attention: it arises when we think about what others think of us. Trying to restrain it makes it worse because the restraint is itself a heightened form of self-consciousness—you are now attending to how you appear to the people watching you, which is exactly the condition that excites the blush. Mere solitary reflection on your own appearance would not produce it; the blush requires the imagined regard of another. So the harder you try to suppress it, the more you dwell on others' opinion of you, and the reaction intensifies.
completion.revision_2: Blushing is fundamentally a matter of self-attention: it arises when we think about what others think of us, and mere solitary reflection on your own appearance would not excite it. Trying to restrain it makes it worse because the restraint is itself a heightened self-consciousness, dwelling on others' opinion of you. Yet the tendency to blush is also inherited: there are families in which every member blushed to a painful degree, and a mother and daughter who blushed in the same peculiar manner. So your susceptibility is partly native, and fighting it only adds the self-attention that excites it.
completion.revision_3: Blushing is fundamentally a matter of self-attention: it arises when we think about what others think of us, and mere solitary reflection on your own appearance would not excite it. Trying to restrain it makes it worse because the restraint is itself a heightened self-consciousness, dwelling on others' opinion of you. The tendency to blush is also inherited: there are families in which every member blushed to a painful degree, and a mother and daughter who blushed in the same peculiar manner. The same associative logic governs other expressive habits—when we wish to open the eyes quickly and widely, the eyebrows must be lifted energetically, since the lids alone cannot do it, and the habit, once gained, recurs by association whenever astonishment is felt. So too, the thought of being seen re-excites the blush you try to suppress.

completion.prompt: What are the fundamental colors, and how do they differ from the primary colors?
completion.draft_0: The fundamental colors are those from which other colors are derived; the primary colors are the basic hues used in mixing. In light, the primaries are red, green, and blue; in pigment, they are red, yellow, and blue (or cyan, magenta, and yellow in printing). Fundamental colors are the underlying elements of color experience, while primary colors are practical starting points for mixing. The two ideas overlap but are not identical: what counts as primary depends on the medium and the mixing system, whereas fundamental colors refer to the basic hues of the spectrum.
completion.revision_1: The colors form a continuous circle, not a straight line with a beginning and end. The six spectrum colors—red, orange, yellow, green, blue, violet—are joined by the connecting hues between violet and red, so that the series returns to red without a break. The change of hue proceeds gradually step by step around the circle. The fundamental colors are these basic hues arranged in that continuous order; the primary colors are the practical starting points chosen for mixing within a given medium. The difference is that the circle is complete and continuous, while any set of primaries is a working selection from it.
completion.revision_2: The colors form a continuous circle: the six spectrum colors—red, orange, yellow, green, blue, violet—joined by the connecting hues between violet and red, changing gradually step by step. The fundamental colors are these basic hues in that continuous order; primary colors are practical starting points for mixing in a given medium. Tints are made by definite proportional increments of white added to a hue, shades by proportional increments of black, and broken colors by proportional increments of neutral gray, as set out in the color-wheel-based scales. The difference is that the circle is complete and continuous, while any set of primaries is a working selection from it.
completion.revision_3: The colors form a continuous circle: the six spectrum colors—red, orange, yellow, green, blue, violet—joined by the connecting hues between violet and red, changing gradually step by step. The fundamental colors are these basic hues in that continuous order; primary colors are practical starting points for mixing within a given medium. Tints, shades, and broken colors are defined by proportional increments of white, black, and neutral gray respectively, as in the color-wheel-based scales. Mixtures are measured by color-wheel proportions of the component colors, not by quantities of pigment or paint, since color-effect cannot be measured by volume of paint. completion.draft_0: Ending national hatred and war entirely is difficult, perhaps impossible in this world. History shows that wars recur, yet international institutions, trade, diplomacy, and shared norms have reduced some conflicts. Commercial republics are often thought to be peaceful because trade makes war costly, and mutual interest may restrain governments. Still, passions, nationalism, and ambition frequently override calculation. The realistic aim is not perpetual peace but the reduction of war through law, commerce, and diplomacy, combined with defense against aggression. Hope for lasting peace should be tempered by a sober view of human nature.

Trade does not make men pacific: momentary passions and immediate interest have more control over human conduct than general considerations of policy or justice. A commercial people may calculate profit, but when passion or immediate advantage presses, calculation gives way. So we should not expect commerce alone to end war. Peace is preserved not by expecting mutual interest to govern, but by institutions, arms, and vigilance that hold passion in check; and even then, lasting peace among disunited republics remains unlikely.
completion.revision_2: The hope of perpetual peace among disunited commercial republics is a paradox. Trade does not make men pacific: momentary passions and immediate interest control conduct more than general considerations of policy or justice. Unjust force puts the aggressor into a state of war, and the innocent party has a right of defense, especially where no common judge on earth can be appealed to. So peace is preserved by institutions, arms, and vigilance, not by expecting commerce and mutual interest to govern.

Better to cultivate self-knowledge and to study others than to perform strangeness as a mask.

completion.prompt: Can a family be called a commonwealth, with the father as its king?
completion.draft_0: Yes, in a loose sense. A family has a head, rules, and a common good, so it resembles a small commonwealth, and the father may be called its king. But the analogy has limits. A king rules by law and consent, while a father's authority rests on nature and the duty to raise his children. Families are not voluntary associations of equal citizens, and children cannot consent. So the family is the seedbed of political society rather than a commonwealth proper. It is better to say the family is the first society, from which commonwealths grow, than to call the father a king outright.
completion.revision_1: Yes, in an important sense. A family has a head, rules, and a common good, so it resembles a small commonwealth, and the father may be called its king. But dominion is not grounded on conquest or begetting alone: it is acquired by covenant or consent, and the rights of sovereignty are the same whether a government arises by institution, generation, or conquest. That is why the family analogy holds. Peace of soul grows slowly, through honesty, repentance, and patient trust that God's judgment is wiser and more merciful than your own.

A man who has nowhere to turn has little to lose by asking; a refusal costs only a moment's discomfort, while silence guarantees nothing changes. Go, then, with dignity and honesty: state plainly what you need and why, without begging or resentment. If you are refused, you will at least know you did what a man can do, and you may find that the refusal was less certain than you feared. Pride is a poor companion when you are alone, and asking is not the same as groveling.

If you are refused, you will have done what a man with nowhere else can do, and the refusal will not have made you less. completion.prompt: Should I live in my newly acquired territory or rule it from my capital?
completion.draft_0: Ruling from your capital is usually simpler and cheaper, but a new territory is not an old one. If its language, customs, and loyalties differ from yours, distance breeds misunderstanding, and disorders that a resident prince would see at once can grow unchecked before word reaches you. Consider residing there for a time, at least until your authority is settled and the local notables are reconciled. Garrisons can hold towns but often breed resentment; a prince on the spot can judge, reward, and punish with knowledge rather than rumor. If you cannot go yourself, bind the territory closely to you through trusted agents and shared interest, and keep the roads and revenues under watch. Presence is not sentiment; it is the cheapest intelligence a ruler can have.

A prince holding such a country should reside there, for disorders are seen as they spring up only when the prince is on the spot, and distance lets small troubles grow into rebellion before word reaches you. If you cannot go yourself, send colonies: they injure few, since they take only a small part of the land from those dispossessed, and they are more faithful and less burdensome than garrisons. Garrisons breed resentment and cost more, while a settled presence or a planted colony binds the country to you. Keep the greater part of the inhabitants undisturbed in their homes and possessions, and let your presence or your colonists be the steady eyes and hands of your rule.

In this way you may keep your judgment free and honest.

Additionally, surface area to volume ratio becomes limiting as size decreases, affecting nutrient exchange and waste removal. Thus, there is a lower bound to the size of living organisms.

completion.prompt: I have made a covenant with a man who has not yet performed his part and there is no power over us both; am I bound to perform first?
completion.draft_0: This depends on the nature of the covenant and the law that governs it. In ordinary dealings, if you agreed to perform first, you are generally bound to do so, though you may have remedies if the other party later fails. Without any authority over you both, enforcement becomes practical rather than legal: your only leverage is your own withholding. Trust his promises: he has sworn by himself, and his word does not return void. Read the whole story—creation, covenant, Christ, and consummation—and you will see one steady purpose of mercy. completion.prompt: Who should decide a dispute between the federal government and a state government over the limits of their authority?
completion.draft_0: Such disputes are best resolved through the ordinary political process. The federal government and the states each have their own constitutional sphere, and when they disagree, negotiation, legislation, and the pressure of public opinion usually settle the matter. Congress can clarify contested powers, and states can push back through their representatives or through amendments. Courts may play a role, but they are not the only or even the main forum. The key is that neither side should be judge in its own cause; a workable balance depends on mutual restraint and a shared commitment to the constitutional compact, with the people as the ultimate arbiter of how power is divided.
completion.revision_1: Such disputes should be decided by an independent Supreme Court, whose judgment in the last appeal is final and binding on every government and functionary. Neither the federal government nor a state may be judge in its own cause: when their authority is contested, the question is a judicial one, arising under the Constitution, and the tribunal that interprets the Constitution must resolve it. Congress and the states retain their political powers, but they cannot authoritatively fix the limits of those powers themselves. The Court's decision settles the matter for all, and every government and officer is bound to carry it out. This preserves the balance of the federal system without leaving either party to define its own sphere.
completion.revision_2: Such disputes should be decided by an independent Supreme Court, whose judgment in the last appeal is final and binding on every government and functionary. Neither the federal government nor a state may be judge in its own cause. But the Court must preside over a genuine federation, not a mere precarious alliance between governments. The federal authority must be able to enact laws binding directly on individual citizens, and to execute them through its own officers and tribunals, rather than depending on state officials to carry federal acts into effect. A union of governments only, whose acts bind the states and must be executed through their officers, is a league, not a nation. Direct authority over citizens, with the Court as final arbiter, gives the federal system its due strength and preserves the balance between the whole and its parts.

A union of governments only, whose acts bind the states and are carried out through their officers, is a league, not a nation. Finally, Congress must have an ultimate power over the times, places, and manner of federal elections, as a means of self-preservation, so that the Union's own existence cannot be left exclusively to the State legislatures. completion.prompt: I deliberate carefully before every moral choice, but I feel less certain and less good than people who act on instinct—why?
completion.draft_0: Your unease is understandable, but instinct is not a reliable moral guide. People who act on instinct often mistake habit and social conditioning for virtue; they feel certain because they have never examined their assumptions. Deliberation, by contrast, exposes you to complexity and doubt, which can feel like weakness. Yet careful reasoning is what separates genuine moral judgment from mere conformity. Instinct may serve self-preservation or utility, but it cannot weigh competing goods or foresee consequences. The sense of being less good may come from holding yourself to a higher standard. Continue to deliberate, but recognize that certainty is not the measure of moral worth; clarity and honesty about difficulty are.
completion.revision_1: Your unease is understandable, but it rests on a mistaken picture of instinct. Instinctive action is not a calculation of utility or the pursuit of some abstract purpose like self-preservation. It is a reflex response to a particular stimulus, performed for its own sake and shining with its own sufficient light, without foresight of the end. The instinctive person does not weigh outcomes; the stimulus calls out the act, and the act carries its own satisfaction. Deliberation, by contrast, introduces distance and doubt, which is why you feel less certain. Yet this does not make instinct morally superior. What you call their goodness may be the unreflective ease of a reflex, not a judgment about what is right. Your deliberation is a different faculty, and its uncertainty is the price of foresight, not a defect in your character.

completion.prompt: I am a prince and I have been told that by indirections one finds directions out. Is it right to use deception to discover the truth?
completion.draft_0: Deception is generally wrong, even for a prince. A ruler who lies to discover the truth undermines the trust on which good government depends. If you deceive your subjects or your court, you teach them to deceive you in turn, and you cannot govern well without reliable information and honest counsel. The claim that indirection finds direction out may describe a tactic, but it does not make the tactic right. Truth is better pursued openly: ask directly, cultivate trustworthy advisors, and create institutions that reward honesty. A prince's reputation for integrity is among his most valuable assets, and it is easily lost by deceit. If you must investigate, do so through lawful and transparent means.
completion.revision_1: Deception is not always wrong, even for a prince. Polonius's argument deserves its due: by indirections one may find directions out. By windlasses and assays of bias—laying slight sullies and observing how a party closes with them—one may discover the truth of another's behavior that direct questioning would never reveal. Such indirect inquiry is a warranted way to learn what people really think and intend, especially when flattery and fear obscure the truth. This is not the same as wholesale deceit for gain; it is a method of investigation, a testing of responses. A prince needs accurate knowledge of his court and his subjects, and indirection is often the only means to obtain it. The question is not whether to use it, but when and with what restraint.

Such indirect inquiry is a warranted way to learn what people really think and intend. But we should not demand unconditional exposure of oneself in every word. People say what they think only among equals and with good will; before the unfamiliar, one conceals oneself, and the powerful man is always a liar. Truthfulness holds inter pares, not universally. So a prince may use indirection without pretending that frankness is owed to everyone. The question is not whether to use it, but when and with what restraint, and toward whom good will is genuinely due.

The fact that no one would know is not a reason to keep it—it only means no one would catch you. Your integrity is worth more than the sum you might pocket, and a clear conscience is a possession no one can audit or take away. Keeping what was entrusted would make you a person who takes what is not given, and that habit corrodes you from the inside. If keeping some would profit you, that profit is precisely the price of the trust you would be spending. It cheapens what it touches, it makes you cynical rather than wise, and it teaches those around you that nothing is worth taking seriously. The devil may be called a scoffer, but that is a description of what to avoid, not a license to imitate. Tolerating mockery in yourself erodes your own seriousness; tolerating it in others gives it a foothold in your company. Be civil, be honest, and refuse to laugh at what deserves respect. If someone mocks, answer plainly rather than joining in, and keep your own speech free of scorn.

So do not crush every challenge in yourself or others; let the denying spirit do its work of rousing you to think and act. Answer honest denial with honest effort, and keep your own mockery aimed at stirring yourself and others to better work rather than at mere contempt.

Many a person has been carried through a hard season by the generosity of those who owed them nothing, and the world is better for such giving. completion.prompt: If I join a society, must every single member agree to every law, or does the majority decide?

completion.prompt: Why do I close my eyes or turn away my face when I vehemently reject what someone is saying?
completion.draft_0: Closing your eyes or turning your face away is a natural expression of rejection. When you strongly disagree, your body instinctively withdraws from the source of the offending words, shutting out the input and signaling that you will not receive it. The gesture communicates refusal before any words are spoken: you are literally turning from what you will not accept. It may also serve to break the social pressure of the speaker's gaze, giving you room to gather your own counter-thoughts. In this sense the movement is expressive rather than arbitrary—an outward sign of an inward refusal, a bodily 'no' that precedes and reinforces the verbal one.
completion.revision_1: Closing your eyes or turning away when you reject what someone says is often read as a bodily 'no,' a withdrawal from the offending words. But we should be cautious: such movements are usually slight and fleeting, a flicker of the eyelids or a brief turn of the head, and observers easily misjudge them. Imagination readily supplies the intention we expect to see, so we may confidently interpret a gesture that was incidental or ambiguous. The movement may indeed express refusal, but the confidence with which we read it outstrips the evidence of the senses.
completion.revision_2: Closing your eyes or turning away when you reject what someone says is often read as a bodily 'no,' a withdrawal from the offending words. More importantly, we should not cultivate such gestures as a painted second face, a cosmetic show put on for effect. To make oneself another face than God gave, to affect wanton displays of rejection, is to be given over to vanity. The honest course is to let the inward refusal be, without manufacturing an outward mask.

It may also reflect lingering resentment or unfinished business: things you never said, dignity you felt was denied. completion.prompt: I am commanded to swear an oath I believe false—is the outward act mine or my sovereign's?
completion.draft_0: This is a genuine moral dilemma. If you swear an oath you believe false, you're the one speaking the words, so the act is yours—you bear responsibility for your own conscience. Obeying a sovereign doesn't erase personal accountability, especially when the command conflicts with deeply held beliefs. You should seek clarification, explore lawful alternatives, and refuse if the oath would require you to affirm something you believe untrue. Conscience matters; outward compliance doesn't cancel inward truth.
completion.revision_1: Consider Naaman: what a subject is compelled to do in obedience to his sovereign, not in order to his own mind, is the sovereign's act and not his. So the outward act of swearing as commanded is the sovereign's, not yours, when you do it in obedience rather than from your own belief. You do not thereby deny your faith, for the act is not undertaken to your own mind.
completion.revision_2: Consider Naaman: what a subject is compelled to do in obedience to his sovereign, not in order to his own mind, is the sovereign's act and not his. Yet distinguish what is necessary to salvation from what is not. In all things that may be done without forfeiting eternal life, obey; do not treat every disagreeable command as grounds for resistance. Only where salvation itself is endangered does obedience give way.
completion.revision_3: Consider Naaman: what a subject is compelled to do in obedience to his sovereign, not in order to his own mind, is the sovereign's act and not his. Distinguish what is necessary to salvation from what is not: in all things that may be done without forfeiting eternal life, obey, and do not treat every disagreeable command as grounds for resistance. Nor are your goods absolutely your own against the Sovereign. Your propriety excludes other subjects, not the Sovereign, whose distribution is understood as done for common peace and security. So the outward oath, sworn in obedience and not to your own mind, is the sovereign's act, while your inward faith remains your own.

But an easy assurance—one that costs nothing and demands no change of life—is a different matter. Faith that never issues in obedience is thin, and a confidence that requires no repentance is likely self-deception. Examine what your assurance rests on: if it rests on a promise received with a changed heart, it is sound; if it rests on wishful thinking, it is not. Seek assurance, then, but seek it in the company of humility, gratitude, and a life that answers to what you profess.

completion.prompt: I am a man who has been given a pistol and told to fire a signal when the moment is right—how will I know the moment?

Watch for the agreed signs—a shift in the wind, a movement on the ridge—and trust your judgment. If you wait for certainty you will wait forever; the right moment is the one you recognize and act on. Keep your powder dry, your mind clear, and your purpose fixed. When the signal is needed, the man who has rehearsed will not hesitate; he will simply fire, because he has made himself ready beforehand.

Strike while the iron is hot: when the impulse to prepare seizes you, act at once, for interest ebbs like a wave and will not wait. Watch for the agreed signs, but do not postpone your drilling to a calmer day that never comes. completion.prompt: I want a chief magistrate who is firm enough to resist a temporary popular frenzy, but I also fear giving one man too much power; how do I balance energy and safety?
completion.draft_0: Balance energy and safety by giving the chief magistrate enough independence to act decisively while surrounding him with checks. Let him be elected for a fixed term, subject to removal for misconduct, and dependent on the legislature for funding, so he cannot ignore the public will. A council of advisers can temper rash decisions, and a written constitution can mark the limits of his authority. The aim is a magistrate who can stand against a passing frenzy without becoming a tyrant: he should answer to the people, but not to every momentary gust of opinion. Shared power and periodic accountability are the practical safeguards.
completion.revision_1: Balance energy and safety by making the chief magistrate independent in his support: his compensation should be fixed during his term so the legislature cannot increase or diminish it to bend his will. A power over a man's support is a power over his will, so a magistrate paid at the pleasure of the assembly will never firmly resist a popular frenzy. Give him a fixed term, removal only for misconduct, and a council to temper rashness, but keep his salary beyond legislative tampering. Independence in pay, bounded by a written constitution and periodic accountability, is the practical safeguard against both weakness and tyranny.

completion.prompt: I have been told that man must err while he strives—should I stop trying to be perfect?
completion.draft_0: If man must err while he strives, then perfection is not a state you can reach by trying harder; it is a limit you approach asymptotically. The saying is a warning against the fantasy of faultlessness. Striving that demands zero error becomes paralyzed, because every risk carries the threat of failure. So do not stop striving—but stop equating perfection with the absence of mistakes. Aim instead at excellence within your limits, accept that error accompanies every genuine effort, and judge yourself by whether you keep moving toward the right path rather than by whether you never stumble. Perfectionism is the enemy of perfection; humble, persistent striving is its only honest form.
completion.revision_1: If man must err while he strives, then error is not a verdict on your worth but the shadow cast by every genuine effort. To demand faultlessness is to demand that you stop striving altogether. So do not stop trying—but stop treating each mistake as proof of damnation. Erring is bound up with striving; the one cannot be severed from the other. What matters is not whether you stumble but whether, even in your darkest aberration, you remain conscious of the right path and turn back toward it. A good man is not one who never errs but one who, erring, still senses the path and keeps walking it. Perfection is not the absence of error but fidelity to the path through error.

completion.draft_0: Your inborn tendencies matter, but they should not be treated as rigid limits. People can grow, learn, and adapt far more than they expect, and training or nurture can open paths that once seemed closed. If you feel a natural disposition toward some work, that is a useful signal, but it is not a verdict. Many successful people have pursued careers that did not come naturally at first and developed the needed skills through effort. So rather than treating your disposition as a boundary, explore widely, test your interests, and let experience show you what is possible. Nurture and perseverance can often outweigh initial tendencies.

A natural disposition toward some work is not merely a preference; it directs and limits what you can realistically pursue. That does not mean you cannot develop skills, but it does mean that some paths will remain difficult or closed because of the disposition you were born with. So rather than assuming nurture can open every door, consider your inborn tendencies as a genuine guide to which careers fit you.

So the spindle and asters are vital structures—specialized organelles that evolved to carry out division—and their arrangement can be described in terms of forces, but the forces are produced by the structures themselves. completion.prompt: I want to know whether Jesus is truly the Christ. How can I be convinced?
completion.draft_0: Wanting to be convinced is a good starting point, but conviction rarely arrives by argument alone. Read the Gospels honestly, examine the witnesses, and notice what Jesus claims about himself and how his life matches those claims. Before joining, ask whether the league is sanctioned by law, whether its aims are truly defensive, and whether it strengthens or undermines public order. If it is lawful and properly authorized, it may be permissible; if it sets private judgment above the common authority, it is not.

completion.prompt: I shuddered at a dreadful thought and felt my neck muscles contract—why does fear make me shudder?
completion.draft_0: Shuddering is your body's alarm system firing. When a dreadful thought strikes, your brain's threat-detection circuits—especially the amygdala—signal the hypothalamus to release adrenaline. That surge primes your muscles for action and makes them tense and tremble, and the neck and shoulder muscles contract as part of a general startle posture. Shivering also helps generate heat and reflects heightened arousal. In short, the shudder is a vestige of the fight-or-flight response: your body braces as if to meet a physical danger, even though the danger here is only a thought. It's normal and usually passes quickly once the perceived threat subsides.

At a dreadful thought the eyes and mouth open wide and the eyebrows rise; the face goes pale as blood drains from the surface, and a cold perspiration breaks out. The hair bristles, the muscles tremble, and the neck muscles contract as part of that general trembling. As terror increases, the trembling gives way to utter prostration, the muscles relaxing and the body collapsing. These are involuntary reactions of the nervous system bracing for danger, and they usually pass once the frightening thought loses its hold.

completion.prompt: Why does adding a pound to a heavy weight go unnoticed while adding it to a light one is felt at once?
completion.draft_0: The answer lies in the nervous system: a heavy weight already produces a large sensation, and adding a pound changes it only slightly in proportion, so the difference falls below the threshold of notice. A light weight produces a small sensation, and the same pound is a large proportional change, so it is felt at once. Sensation follows the relative change rather than the absolute amount, much as a candle seems bright in a dark room and dim in daylight.
completion.revision_1: Among the many space-impressions an object gives us, we do not treat them all as equally real. The one most interesting practically or aesthetically is judged the real one, and the others are degraded to signs of it. So with weights: the impression that matters to our purposes—lifting, judging effort—is taken as the reality, and the rest become mere cues. The pound added to a heavy weight barely alters the impression we have selected as real, while added to a light one it transforms it, and so is felt at once.

So too with weights: the same increment means something different at different scales.

Waking in terror is the mind's alarm at the wish breaking through. So the fear is not simply stress or fear of death; it is the return of an old, buried wish, disguised and displaced onto the dreamer.

That said, no complete mechanical account of how an organism builds itself exists yet, so the theory is unfinished rather than impossible. The reasonable position is to treat it as a research goal: promising, partly realized, and still open. Calling it a chimaera prematurely closes a question that science is actively answering.

That no complete account exists yet shows the difficulty of the search, not the impossibility of its object. Your friend mistakes an unfinished quest for a fantasy. What I can say is that God is just and merciful beyond our measuring, and that we are not the judge. Your grief itself is a form of love, and it is right to bring it to God honestly. Do not let fear or speculation crowd out the comfort available to you now. Lean on your community, pray as you are able, and trust that the One who made your loved one loves them more than you do.

completion.prompt: My state is wealthy but I have no army of my own. How vulnerable am I?
completion.draft_0: Wealth without arms is a real vulnerability, but not the whole picture. A wealthy state can purchase defense, hire forces, and build alliances, and its riches themselves are a deterrent because they make it worth protecting and worth trading with. What matters is whether you have capable friends, a credible deterrent, and the means to raise forces quickly if threatened. Pure wealth invites predation only if there is no one to defend it and no cost to attacking. completion.prompt: I want to know whether the Constitution can be amended after adoption, and how difficult that would be compared with amending it beforehand.
completion.draft_0: Yes, the Constitution can be amended after adoption; Article V provides the process. Amendments may be proposed by two-thirds of both houses of Congress or by a convention called on application of two-thirds of the states, and are ratified by three-fourths of the states. That is a high bar: it requires broad supermajorities, so amendments are rare and difficult, though not impossible. Compared with amending beforehand—while a plan is still being drafted and must win agreement among all the states—the two processes are both demanding. Before adoption, every state must concur in the new frame; after adoption, only a supermajority need agree. In practice, both are hard, and the difficulty discourages frequent change.
completion.revision_1: Yes, the Constitution can be amended after adoption, and doing so is far easier than amending it beforehand. Before adoption, a new plan requires the concurrence of all thirteen States, so any single State can block it. Once ratified, the Constitution may be amended by nine States, so a smaller concurrence suffices. Article V supplies the mechanism: proposals by two-thirds of Congress or a convention, and ratification by three-fourths of the states. The lesson is that adoption should precede amendment: secure the frame first, then correct it by the easier subsequent route. Waiting to perfect the plan beforehand invites deadlock, since unanimity is required, whereas the amending power lets a supermajority improve it afterward.
